question.text: The 1987 UN Brundtland Commission defined sustainability as:

answer.text: Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Achieving financial profits while investing a minimum of 2% in CSR
Maximising GDP growth over a 25-year horizon
Reducing carbon emissions to net-zero by 2030

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Ch 1.5.1 (v), the UN Brundtland Commission 1987 defined sustainability as 'meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs'. This is the foundational definition across environmental, social and economic dimensions. The Trap: Option B conflates CSR with sustainability. Option C is a growth statement, not sustainability. Option D references a specific target (net-zero 2030), not the Brundtland definition. Cross-Exam Context: Cross-links to Ch 6 (Frameworks — GRI, SASB) where Brundtland underpins ESG reporting. SIAs cite this in SAS-500 environmental assurance engagements. Assessor's Pro-Tip: For SAS-500 engagements, triangulate the SE's sustainability claim against the 3-pillar (environment/society/economy) nested model. Weak social or economic performance can undermine even strong environmental outputs — test for balance.
